common_name: Virginia Jumbo Peanut (Large-Seeded Southern Boiling Peanut)

planting.note: Direct sow shelled, raw (untreated) seed into warm soil once nights stay above 60°F; peanuts need a long, warm, frost-free season, which makes the extended Gulf Coast growing season an excellent fit.

directions: Plant shelled seed about an inch and a half deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, since peanuts push their flower stalks ('pegs') down into the soil to form pods underground and need friable soil for those pegs to penetrate easily. Virginia Jumbo is the classic large-seeded Virginia-type peanut behind most of the boiled and roasted-in-shell peanuts sold across the South, prized for producing the biggest pods and kernels of any common peanut type, typically two large seeds per pod. Hill soil slightly around the base of plants as they grow to give pegs an easier path into the ground, and keep soil evenly moist through flowering and peg development, since drought stress at that stage sharply reduces yield. Dig the whole plant once leaves begin yellowing in fall, and cure pods in a warm, airy spot for one to two weeks before shelling or storing.

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 65°F; benne thrives in the long, hot, humid Gulf Coast summer that many other crops struggle with, and is notably drought-tolerant once established.

directions: Sow seed a quarter-inch deep in warm, well-drained soil once the danger of frost has passed and soil has thoroughly warmed. Benne is the historic name for sesame brought to the South Carolina Lowcountry by enslaved West Africans, who carried both the seed and the West African Bantu word 'benne' for it, and who used it in traditional dishes and confections that remain part of Lowcountry foodways today, most famously benne wafers and benne brittle. The tall, branching plants produce small tubular flowers followed by seed pods that split open when fully dry, releasing the small, flavorful seeds prized both toasted for cooking and pressed for oil. Benne is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, thriving in conditions that stress many other summer crops, and needs relatively little care beyond weeding while young. Harvest whole seed stalks once the lower pods begin to split, and finish drying upside down in a paper bag to catch seed as pods open.
sources: Anson Mills — heirloom benne seed history

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil once all frost danger has passed; Sugar Drip is a tall, long-season sweet sorghum that benefits from the Gulf Coast's long, hot growing season to fully load the stalks with sugar before harvest.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in rows in fertile, well-drained soil once the soil has warmed, thinning seedlings to their final spacing. Sugar Drip is a classic Southern heirloom sweet sorghum, grown not for grain but for its tall, juicy canes, which are cut, crushed, and boiled down into sorghum syrup — a traditional sweetener across the rural South before cane sugar became widely available and still prized today for its distinctive, robust, molasses-like flavor. Plants grow into tall, cane-like stalks resembling corn, topped with a grain head that can be left for birds or harvested for feed once the syrup-bearing stalks are cut. Harvest when seed heads reach the hard-dough stage and stalks are packed with sweet juice, typically signaled by the lower leaves beginning to dry; press stalks promptly after cutting, since sugar content declines quickly once cut canes sit.

common_name: Greasy Back Bean (Appalachian Heirloom Cornfield Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis, corn stalks, or other tall support; this vigorous climbing pole bean traditionally grown alongside corn needs sturdy support to reach its full length.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep at the base of a trellis or tall support in fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Greasy Back belongs to a distinctive family of Appalachian heirloom 'greasy bean' varieties named for pods that lack the fine fuzz found on most bean pods, giving them a smooth, shiny, almost oiled appearance that is unmistakable at a glance. Traditionally grown climbing up corn stalks in mountain garden plots, the vigorous vines produce tender, flavorful pods that can be picked young as snap beans, allowed to mature further for flavorful fresh shell beans, or left to dry fully for a rich, hearty dry bean prized in Appalachian cooking. Pick regularly to keep vines productive over a long season, and let the last flush of pods dry on the vine if a dry bean harvest is wanted.

common_name: Mountaineer Half Runner Bean (West Virginia Heirloom Half-Runner)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost; half-runner types produce short runners longer than a true bush bean but shorter than a full pole bean, and benefit from light staking or a low trellis even though they can be grown unsupported.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after last frost, providing light support such as a low trellis or twiggy brush for the heaviest yields. Mountaineer is a West Virginia Appalachian heirloom half-runner bean, a growth habit intermediate between bush and pole types that produces short climbing runners while still setting a concentrated, earlier harvest more like a bush bean. The tender, stringless, flavorful pods are a favorite for fresh eating and traditional Appalachian canning and pickling ('leather britches' style stringing and drying is also common with half-runner types), and the plants tend to keep producing over a longer window than most bush beans. Pick regularly once pods reach full size but before seeds bulge visibly inside, since frequent picking is the single most effective way to keep any snap bean, including half-runners, producing longer.
